lines.text: The last structure answered one specific question well: a running sum, one operator, nothing but one array and a little bit arithmetic.
But it has real limits. It can't tell you the smallest value in a stretch, and it can't apply one correction across an entire stretch at once.
This topic builds the structure that closes both gaps, for any operator that makes sense to combine, not just a sum.
Here's the one new picture this topic needs: a small binary tree, drawn above the array itself.
Every leaf holds one slot's own value. Every node above a leaf holds whatever its two children combine to.
Built once, from the bottom up — each node combines its own two children exactly once, nothing recomputed twice.
Before the reveal, a natural first guess is that answering a question about a stretch of positions means visiting a node for every position in it.
Ask instead whether the tree can skip straight past any branch whose own stretch doesn't matter at all.
A handful of nodes, not one per position and not the whole tree.
Doubling how many positions the array holds would only add one more level to climb, not many more nodes to visit.
Watch the descent: any branch whose own stretch sits entirely inside the question gets used directly, no further.
Any branch whose own stretch sits entirely outside the question gets skipped without a second look.
Only a branch straddling the edge of the question gets split open to look further.
Here's the generalization the whole topic is built around: swap out the one operator plugged into every node's combine step, and the identical tree answers a different question.
Nothing about where the nodes sit, or how the descent skips branches, changes at all.
The identical structure, stored a second way: one flat list, no pointers, no recursion, each position's own neighbor fixed in advance by simple arithmetic.
A single position's own update climbs straight from its own leaf to the root, combining with its sibling at every step on the way up.
Same answers, every time, on every question — only how the structure is kept in memory changed.
Before this reveal, notice the instinct: correcting an entire stretch at once sounds like it should cost one touch per position in that stretch.
Ask instead whether a single tag, sitting at one node whose own stretch already matches the correction, could stand in for touching every position underneath it.
It can, and it does: one tag, at one node, costing what a single-position update costs.
Nothing underneath that node gets touched at all, not yet.
A tag sits at a node on purpose, marking its entire stretch as corrected without visiting one position beneath it.
It stays there until some later question actually needs to see past that node and down into its own children.
Only then does the tag move down one level, handed off to both children before the question continues.

tolerated.line: Only then does the tag move down one level, handed off to both children before the question continues.

lines.text: Here's the one place getting this wrong would actually break something real.
A node already carries one kind of pending correction. A second, different kind of correction arrives for the identical node before either one has moved down. Which one survives?
If the new correction simply overwrites the old base value outright, ask whether an earlier, still-pending adjustment to that value should still apply afterward, or whether it's simply gone.
An overwrite discards whatever adjustment was pending before it — the old base value is gone, so an adjustment to it no longer means anything.

The reverse direction behaves differently: a later adjustment, arriving after an overwrite is already pending, folds straight into that overwrite's own value instead of sitting beside it as a second, separate correction.
Here's where the real cost gets checked against a count, not an argument.
Across the same batch of stretch-wide corrections on the identical array, a version with no deferred tags touched every single position in every stretch, every time.
The version with deferred tags touched only a small, bounded handful of nodes per correction — the saving this whole mechanism exists to deliver, measured directly.
